short: The base class for almost every engine type, which gives a class reflection, garbage collection, and editor support.
long: Think of UObject as the membership card for the engine's club. Once your class derives from it, the engine can list its properties in the editor, save it to disk, find it by name, and clean it up when nothing uses it anymore. Data-only classes such as a quest definition or an inventory item rule usually derive straight from UObject, while things that live in a level derive from AActor, which is itself a UObject. Class names that start with U, like UHealthComponent, signal a UObject that is not an actor.

short: Any object that can be placed in or spawned into a level, such as a door, a pickup, a light, or a character.
long: An actor is a container that exists in the world and owns a set of components that give it shape and behavior. On its own it has no mesh or position; its root component supplies the transform. A pressure plate actor might own a box component to detect feet and a static mesh component so you can see it. Actors get lifecycle calls like BeginPlay, Tick, and EndPlay, can replicate over the network, and are created at runtime with SpawnActor rather than NewObject.

short: An actor that a player or an AI can control, like a vehicle, a turret, or a floating camera.
long: A pawn is the body, and a controller is the mind that drives it. The pawn holds the physical representation and reacts to commands, while the controller decides what those commands are. A tank in a strategy game could be a pawn possessed by a player controller in one match and by an AI controller in another, with no change to the tank class itself. If you need walking, jumping, and a skeletal mesh out of the box, use the Character subclass instead.

short: A ready-made pawn for walking creatures that comes with a capsule, a skeletal mesh, and a movement component.
long: ACharacter saves you from building humanoid movement by hand. It ships with a capsule for collision, a skeletal mesh slot for the visible body, an arrow showing which way is forward, and the Character Movement Component that handles walking, falling, jumping, swimming, and network smoothing. A hero, an enemy grunt, and a shopkeeper NPC are all good fits. A good habit is to put shared stats in a common parent such as ADojoCharacter so player and enemy classes do not duplicate code.

short: A reusable piece of behavior that you attach to an actor, with no position of its own.
long: Components let you build actors from parts instead of deep inheritance trees. A UActorComponent holds logic or data but has no transform, which makes it ideal for things like a health pool, an inventory, or a quest tracker. Drop a UHealthComponent onto a barrel, a boss, and a player and all three can take damage the same way. If the part needs a location in the world, such as a muzzle point or a trigger volume, use a scene component instead.

short: A component that has a transform and can be attached to other scene components in a parent and child tree.
long: A scene component adds location, rotation, and scale to the component idea. Scene components form a hierarchy: when the parent moves, the children follow. On a turret, an empty scene component called MuzzlePoint can sit at the end of the barrel so projectiles always spawn from the right place, even while the barrel rotates. You set up the tree in a constructor with SetupAttachment, or at runtime with AttachToComponent.

short: A scene component that has geometry, so it can be drawn, collide, or simulate physics.
long: Primitive components are the scene components that physically matter. Meshes and collision shapes such as boxes, spheres, and capsules all derive from UPrimitiveComponent, which is where collision settings, overlap and hit events, and physics simulation live. When an overlap event fires, the engine hands you the UPrimitiveComponent that was touched, so you can tell whether a sword hit the enemy's capsule or a separate weak-point sphere.

short: A component that draws a rigid 3D model, like a crate, a sword, or a wall.
long: A static mesh is a model that does not bend with bones. The component places one of these models in the world and can also provide collision from the mesh's simple collision shapes. A pickup actor might use a box component as its root for clean overlap detection and a static mesh component as a child to show the item spinning. Turning off collision on the mesh when a simpler shape already handles it is a common, cheap performance win.

short: A component that draws a model driven by a skeleton of bones, so it can be animated.
long: Characters, creatures, and anything that bends use a skeletal mesh. The component plays animations through an animation blueprint, exposes bones and sockets you can attach things to, and can drive a physics asset for ragdolls. On an ACharacter you reach it with GetMesh(). If you want a sword in the hero's right hand, you attach the sword actor to a socket on this component, and the sword follows every swing of the arm.

short: A pill-shaped collision shape, used by characters because it slides smoothly over steps and edges.
long: The capsule is the invisible pill that a character actually collides with. Its rounded ends let movement glide over small bumps instead of snagging the way a box would. ACharacter makes it the root component, so its size defines how tall and wide your character is for doors and corridors. Overlap checks against the capsule are much cheaper than checking against every triangle of the skeletal mesh, which is why the mesh is often set to no collision.

short: A box-shaped collision shape, often used as a trigger zone or a simple blocker.
long: A box component is the go-to shape for rectangular areas: a doorway trigger, a pressure plate, a kill zone under the map, or a solid crate. You set its half-size with SetBoxExtent. Set to overlap, it fires begin and end overlap events when a pawn walks in or out; set to block, it stops movement and fires hit events. Making it the root of a small actor gives clean, predictable collision regardless of what the mesh looks like.

short: A ball-shaped collision shape, common for pickup radii, detection ranges, and projectiles.
long: A sphere is the cheapest shape to test, so it is great for radius checks. A defense tower can use a large overlapping sphere as its aggro range: when the player enters, the tower starts firing, and when the player leaves, it stops. A small blocking sphere also makes a good root for a projectile because its shape looks the same from every direction. Change the size at runtime with SetSphereRadius.

short: A component that defines a viewpoint, so the player sees the world from where it sits.
long: When a player controller possesses a pawn, the view usually comes from a camera component on that pawn. You set field of view and projection on it, and it is almost always attached to a spring arm so it can trail behind or hover above the character. For a top-down game, the camera hangs high on a long spring arm pitched downward; for a first-person game, it sits at eye height and uses the controller's rotation.

short: A component that holds a camera at a set distance and pulls it closer when something blocks the view.
long: Picture a selfie stick with a spring in it. The spring arm keeps its child, usually a camera, a fixed length away from the character, and if a wall gets in the way it shortens so the camera never clips through geometry. Key settings are TargetArmLength, whether it tests collision, whether it uses the pawn's control rotation, and optional lag so the camera trails smoothly. Attach the camera to the arm's end with USpringArmComponent::SocketName.

short: The component that moves a Character: walking, falling, jumping, swimming, and smoothing it over the network.
long: This is one of the biggest systems in the engine, and you rarely need to rewrite it. You tune it: MaxWalkSpeed for how fast an enemy chases, JumpZVelocity for jump height, bOrientRotationToMovement so a top-down hero turns toward where it runs, and RotationRate for how fast it turns. Its Velocity tells you how fast the character is moving, which is handy for feeding a locomotion blend space. It also handles client prediction so player movement feels responsive online.

short: A character function that throws the character with a velocity you give it, the usual starting point for dashes, jump pads, and knockbacks.
long: LaunchCharacter(Velocity, bXYOverride, bZOverride) hands a velocity to the Character Movement Component, which applies it on the next movement update and always switches the character to falling until it lands again, even when the push is flat along the ground. The two flags choose whether the new velocity replaces the current one on the flat axes and on the vertical axis, or is added to it; a dash usually replaces the flat part so it feels the same at a standstill and at a run. Because the movement component does the moving, it sweeps the capsule and never passes through a wall, but a launched character that meets a wall at an angle slides along it and keeps its speed, so a dash that must end at a wall needs a sweep first or a reaction to the hit.

short: A component that flies its actor forward with speed, gravity, bouncing, or homing, without you writing movement code.
long: Set an initial speed, a max speed, and a gravity scale, and the actor flies. Turn on bouncing for grenades, or homing for a seeking missile. It moves the root component with sweeps, so a blocking collision shape on the root will stop it and fire a hit event, which avoids fast bullets tunneling through thin walls. Writing the same motion by hand in Tick is a good exercise, but this component is the production choice for most projectiles.

short: The actor that owns the rules of a match and decides which pawn, controller, and state classes players get.
long: The game mode is the referee. It picks the default pawn class, player controller class, game state class, and player state class, decides where players spawn, and holds rules such as win conditions or respawn timing. It exists only on the server in multiplayer, so clients cannot read it; anything clients must see belongs in the game state. AGameModeBase is the lean version; AGameMode adds match states like waiting to start and in progress.

short: The actor that holds match-wide information every player should know, such as the clock or the team score.
long: If the game mode is the referee, the game state is the scoreboard everyone can see. It exists on the server and on every client and replicates its marked properties, which makes it the right home for a countdown timer, the current wave number, or whether the base has fallen. Keep rules out of it and keep shared facts in it. Your game mode tells the engine to use your class through GameStateClass.

short: The invisible actor that represents a human player, turns their input into commands, and possesses a pawn.
long: The player controller is the player's will in the game. It survives when the pawn dies, so it is a good place for input handling that should not reset, camera control, showing the mouse cursor, and opening menus. It possesses one pawn at a time and can switch pawns, for example when the player climbs into a vehicle. In multiplayer each client has its own controller, and the server has one for every player.

short: A replicated actor that stores one player's public info, such as name, score, or team, and survives respawns.
long: Each player gets a player state, and every machine in a multiplayer session can see all of them, which makes it perfect for a scoreboard. Because it is not the pawn, a player's kill count does not reset when their character dies and respawns. Private or local-only data, such as unsaved settings, does not belong here. Reach it from a pawn with GetPlayerState, or from the game state's PlayerArray.

short: A single object created when the game launches that survives every level change until the game closes.
long: Levels come and go, but the game instance stays. That makes it a natural home for things that span maps: the chosen character, menu-to-match handoff, or host and join functions that open a level with the listen option. Each running copy of the game has its own instance, server included, and it is not replicated, so it is not a way to share data across the network. For organized session-wide services, prefer a game instance subsystem over piling code into this class.

short: An engine-managed singleton whose lifetime is tied to a host, such as the game instance or the world.
long: Subsystems give you a clean place for a manager without writing singleton code. Derive from the right base, and the engine creates your object when the host starts and destroys it when the host ends, with Initialize and Deinitialize hooks. Need a quest log that survives level loads? Use a game instance subsystem. Need a per-level spawn director? Use a world subsystem. You fetch one with GetSubsystem on its host, and Blueprints can reach them too.

short: A subsystem that lives as long as the game instance, so it persists across level changes.
long: Use this for services the whole play session needs: a save manager, an achievement tracker, or a quest log. It is created right after the game instance starts and cleaned up when the game closes. Access it with GetGameInstance()->GetSubsystem<UDojoQuestSubsystem>(). Compared with putting the same code on the game instance class, subsystems keep each responsibility in its own small class, which follows the single responsibility idea.

short: A subsystem created for each world, so it resets whenever a new level loads.
long: A world subsystem is the right owner for things that belong to the current map: tracking every active enemy, a spawn director, or a registry of interactable objects. Because each world gets its own copy, data never leaks from one level into the next. Grab it with GetWorld()->GetSubsystem<T>(). There is also a tickable variant if the manager needs to update every frame without being an actor.

short: A subsystem created for each local player on this machine, used for per-player services like input mappings.
long: In split-screen, two people share one machine, and each needs their own settings. A local player subsystem gives each of them a separate instance. The best-known example is the Enhanced Input subsystem, where you add an input mapping context for that specific player. You reach it through the local player, usually by asking the player controller for GetLocalPlayer() and then calling GetSubsystem.

short: A subsystem that lives as long as the engine itself, in both the editor and the running game.
long: Engine subsystems start before any game instance or world exists and end only when the engine shuts down. They suit low-level services that do not care which level or session is active, such as a custom analytics pipe or a hardware integration. Most gameplay code never needs one; reach for a game instance or world subsystem first. Access is through GEngine->GetEngineSubsystem<T>().

short: A subsystem that exists only inside the Unreal Editor, for building tools rather than gameplay.
long: If you are writing an editor tool, such as a batch renamer for assets or a level validation pass, an editor subsystem gives it a managed home. It never exists in a packaged game, so its code must live in an editor-only module or be wrapped so it does not ship. Access it with GEditor->GetEditorSubsystem<T>(). Many built-in editor features, like asset and level editing helpers, are exposed this way.

short: The top-level object for everything currently in play: loaded levels, actors, physics, timers, and networking.
long: When you press Play, the engine creates a world and loads levels into it. Nearly everything that touches the running game goes through the world: SpawnActor, line traces, the timer manager, and finding the game mode or game state. From any actor or component you can call GetWorld(). In the editor there may be several worlds at once, such as the editor world and one play-in-editor world per player, which is a reason never to cache a world pointer in static data.

short: One map's collection of placed actors, saved as an asset and loaded into a world.
long: A level is what you edit in the viewport: the terrain, lights, enemies, and triggers you placed. A world always has a persistent level and can stream other levels in and out, and large UE5 maps often use World Partition to stream cells automatically. In menus, you move between levels with OpenLevel, for example from a lobby map to a battle map. Each level can also have its own Level Blueprint for map-specific scripting.

short: The macro placed above a class to register it with the reflection system so the engine and Blueprints can see it.
long: Writing UCLASS() above a class that derives from UObject tells the build tools to generate the hidden code that makes the class known to the engine. Specifiers inside the parentheses change how it behaves: Blueprintable lets designers make Blueprint children, BlueprintType lets it be used as a Blueprint variable type, Abstract stops it from being placed directly, and meta=(BlueprintSpawnableComponent) puts a component in the Add Component menu. The class also needs GENERATED_BODY() and the matching .generated.h include.

short: The macro that registers a plain data struct with reflection so it can be edited, saved, replicated, and used in Blueprints.
long: A USTRUCT is a bundle of values, such as an FLootDrop with an item class, a chance, and a count. It is a value type: copying it copies the data, and it is not garbage collected on its own. Mark it USTRUCT(BlueprintType), add GENERATED_BODY(), and give its fields UPROPERTY so they show in the editor. Structs are the building block of data table rows and are a good choice whenever you need grouped data without the overhead of a full UObject.

short: The macro that registers an enum so it shows as a dropdown in the editor and can be used in Blueprints.
long: An enum names a small set of choices, such as a character state of Locomotion, Attack, Hit, or Die. Unreal style is an enum class with a byte base type: UENUM(BlueprintType) enum class ECharacterState : uint8 { ... }. The uint8 keeps it small and is required for Blueprint use. UMETA(DisplayName = "Knocked Out") on a value changes the label designers see. Enums pair well with a switch statement and with state machines.

short: The macro above a member variable that makes the engine aware of it for editing, saving, Blueprints, networking, and garbage collection.
long: A plain C++ member is invisible to the engine. Add UPROPERTY and it can appear in the Details panel, be read or written by Blueprints, be saved with the level, replicate, and, for UObject pointers, keep the referenced object alive during garbage collection. Specifiers control each of those: UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere, BlueprintReadOnly, Category = "Combat") float Damage = 10.f; A safe rule for beginners is that every UObject pointer you store in a class member gets a UPROPERTY.

short: A property specifier that lets designers change the value in the editor, both on the class defaults and on placed instances.
long: EditAnywhere turns a variable into a tuning knob. Put it on a tower's AttackRange and a designer can make one tower long range and another short range without touching code. Its siblings narrow where the knob appears: EditDefaultsOnly shows it only on the Blueprint class defaults, which is good for values that should be the same for every copy, and EditInstanceOnly shows it only on individual actors placed in a level.

short: A property specifier that shows a value in the editor but does not let anyone change the pointer or value itself.
long: Use VisibleAnywhere for things designers should see but not replace. The classic case is a component pointer created in the constructor: the designer can select the mesh component and change its settings, but cannot swap out the component pointer. The variants VisibleDefaultsOnly and VisibleInstanceOnly limit where it shows, just like the edit specifiers. It is often paired with BlueprintReadOnly so graphs can use the component.

short: A property specifier that lets Blueprint graphs both read and change the variable.
long: With BlueprintReadWrite, a Blueprint gets both a Get node and a Set node for the variable. That is useful for values designers script against, such as an animation instance's Speed. It also means any graph can change the value without your C++ knowing, so for values with rules, like health that must stay between zero and max, prefer BlueprintReadOnly plus a BlueprintCallable setter that enforces the rule.

short: A property specifier that lets Blueprint graphs read a variable but not change it.
long: BlueprintReadOnly gives graphs a Get node and nothing else. It is the safe default for anything owned by C++ logic: current health, a cached target, or a component pointer. Designers can display the value in a health bar or branch on it, while the rules for changing it stay in one place in your code. On a private member, add meta=(AllowPrivateAccess = "true") so Blueprints are allowed to see it.

short: A specifier that groups a property or function under a heading in the editor and in Blueprint menus.
long: Category = "Combat" puts a variable under a Combat heading in the Details panel, and puts a function under that heading in the Blueprint action menu. A pipe makes nested groups, as in Category = "Dojo|Combat". It sounds cosmetic, but on a class with thirty tunable values it is the difference between a designer finding AttackRange in two seconds or scrolling forever.

short: Extra key and value hints inside UPROPERTY, UFUNCTION, or UCLASS that change how the editor and Blueprints present something.
long: Metadata is mostly about the editor experience. meta=(ClampMin = "0", ClampMax = "100") stops a designer from typing a negative health value, DisplayName renames a label, AllowPrivateAccess exposes a private member to Blueprints, BindWidget links a C++ widget pointer to a named widget in the designer, and EditCondition greys a field out unless a checkbox is on. Metadata is for tooling; most of it does not exist in a packaged game, so do not rely on it for gameplay rules.

short: A metadata key that lets Blueprints see a property even though it is private in C++.
long: Good C++ keeps members private, but Blueprints normally only see public or protected members. AllowPrivateAccess bridges that gap. A common pattern is a private component pointer marked VisibleAnywhere, BlueprintReadOnly, meta=(AllowPrivateAccess = "true"), plus a public inline getter for other C++ code. Outside code cannot reassign it, yet designers can still use the component in graphs.

short: A metadata key that changes the label the editor shows for a property, function, class, or enum value.
long: Code names and designer-friendly names do not always match. DisplayName lets a function called GetHealthPoints appear as Get HP in Blueprint search, or an enum value called KnockedOut appear as Knocked Out. Only the label changes; the C++ name and any saved data stay the same. Use it sparingly so the code and the editor do not drift so far apart that people cannot find one from the other.

short: The macro above a function declaration that registers it with the engine, for Blueprints, delegates, networking, or console use.
long: A UFUNCTION is a function the engine can find by name at runtime. That is what lets a Blueprint call it, a dynamic delegate bind to it, a timer call it by name, or the network route it as an RPC. Even with empty parentheses it matters: a function you pass to AddDynamic for an overlap event must be a UFUNCTION or the binding silently fails. Specifiers such as BlueprintCallable, BlueprintPure, BlueprintImplementableEvent, BlueprintNativeEvent, Server, and Client set its role.

short: A function specifier that lets Blueprint graphs call a C++ function as a node with execution pins.
long: BlueprintCallable is how C++ hands tools to designers. Write the hard logic once, such as StartListenServer or ApplyDamageWithArmor, and mark it callable, and it appears as a node they can drop into any graph. Callable nodes have white execution pins, so they run in a specific order and are allowed to change state. If a function only reads data and changes nothing, BlueprintPure is usually the better fit.

short: A function specifier for getters that change nothing, shown in Blueprints as a node without execution pins.
long: A pure node is like a formula cell in a spreadsheet: it has inputs and outputs but no place in the execution chain. GetHealthPercent or IsDead are good examples. One thing to know is that a pure node runs again every time something reads its output, so an expensive pure function wired to three places runs three times. Keep pure functions cheap, and mark the C++ function const as a reminder that it must not change the object.

short: A function specifier for a hook that C++ calls but a Blueprint fills in; you write no C++ body.
long: This is C++ saying: something happens here, designer, you decide what it looks like. Declare UFUNCTION(BlueprintImplementableEvent) void OnLevelUp(int32 NewLevel); and call it from C++ when the player levels up. A Blueprint child adds the event and plays a sound, spawns sparkles, or shows a banner. If no Blueprint implements it, the call does nothing. You must not write a C++ definition for it; the build tools generate one.

short: A function specifier for a hook with a default C++ body that a Blueprint may override.
long: Use this when C++ should provide sensible default behavior but designers might want to replace it. You declare UFUNCTION(BlueprintNativeEvent) void OnHit(); and then write the body as OnHit_Implementation(). Callers still call OnHit(), and the engine routes the call to the Blueprint override if one exists, or to your _Implementation otherwise. Inside a Blueprint override, the designer can call the parent node to run your C++ version too.

short: A function a client calls that actually runs on the server, used to ask the server to do something.
long: Clients cannot change authoritative game state directly, so they ask. Declare UFUNCTION(Server, Reliable) void ServerAttack(); and implement ServerAttack_Implementation(). When the owning client calls ServerAttack, the request travels to the server, which runs the body and decides what really happens. The call only works on actors the client owns, such as its player controller or possessed pawn. Treat every server RPC as a request that might be cheating and check it.

short: A function the server calls that runs only on the client that owns the actor.
long: A client RPC is a private message from the server to one player. It is perfect for things only that player should experience: a screen shake when they are hit, a personal reward popup, or a tutorial hint. Declare it with UFUNCTION(Client, Reliable) and implement the _Implementation body. If what you want is for everyone to see something, use a multicast RPC or a replicated property instead.

short: A function the server calls that runs on the server and on every connected client.
long: Multicast is the server shouting to the whole room. It suits one-off cosmetic events that everyone should see right now, like an explosion effect or an attack animation starting. It is a poor fit for lasting state: a player who joins after the shout never hears it. For state that must stay correct, such as whether a door is open, use a replicated property with RepNotify, and keep multicasts for moments.

short: RPC specifiers that choose whether a message is guaranteed to arrive or may be dropped to save bandwidth.
long: Reliable RPCs are resent until they arrive, in order, which you want for important events like using an item or confirming a purchase. Unreliable RPCs may be dropped under load, which is fine for frequent cosmetic updates where the next message replaces the last one anyway. Sending reliable RPCs every frame can clog the connection, so do not mark a Tick-rate message as reliable.

short: A macro placed at the top of every reflected class or struct body, where the build tools insert generated code.
long: When the build runs, the header tool writes boilerplate for each reflected type: type registration, constructors it needs, and glue for Blueprints and networking. GENERATED_BODY() is the slot where that code is pasted in. Put it as the first line inside the class or struct braces. If you forget it, or the .generated.h include is missing, you get confusing compile errors that mention generated code rather than your mistake.

short: The header the build tools create for each reflected file, which must be the last include in that header.
long: Every header that declares a UCLASS, USTRUCT, or UENUM must include its own generated header, named after the file, such as #include "DojoDoor.generated.h". It has to be the final include, after CoreMinimal and any base class headers, because the generated code depends on everything above it. Adding another include below it is one of the most common first-week compile errors.

short: The build step that reads your reflection macros and writes the generated code that makes them work.
long: Before the C++ compiler sees your files, the Unreal Header Tool scans headers for UCLASS, UPROPERTY, UFUNCTION, and friends, and writes the .generated.h and .gen.cpp files. That is why reflection macros must use exact syntax: the header tool parses them itself and reports errors such as an unknown specifier. Errors that start with the header file name and mention a macro usually come from this step, not from the compiler.

short: A hidden template instance of each class, built by running its constructor once, that new instances copy their defaults from.
long: When the engine starts, it constructs one default object per class. Every actor you spawn or place starts as a copy of that template, then applies any edits made in the editor. This explains a key rule: the constructor runs to build the template, often before any world exists, so it should only set defaults and create components, never find other actors or start gameplay. Gameplay setup belongs in BeginPlay. You can read a class's defaults with GetDefault<T>().

short: The engine's ability to inspect classes, properties, and functions at runtime, powered by the U macros.
long: Standard C++ forgets type details once the code is compiled. Unreal's reflection keeps a catalog: for each reflected class it knows the property names, their types, the functions, and the metadata. That catalog powers the Details panel, Blueprint nodes, saving and loading, replication, and garbage collection tracking. You opt in with UCLASS, USTRUCT, UENUM, UPROPERTY, and UFUNCTION, and anything without a macro is invisible to all of those systems.

short: The engine system that frees UObjects automatically once nothing reachable refers to them anymore.
long: You do not delete UObjects yourself. Every so often the collector starts from a set of roots, follows every reflected reference, and frees anything it could not reach. The catch is that it only sees references it knows about: a UObject pointer stored in a UPROPERTY, a reflected container, or a few special holders. A raw pointer without UPROPERTY does not keep the object alive and can end up pointing at freed memory. Forcing a collection by hand is expensive and rarely needed.

short: The UE5 wrapper for UObject pointers stored as class members, which works like a raw pointer but adds editor tracking.
long: In UE5, a member like UPROPERTY() TObjectPtr<UStaticMeshComponent> Mesh; replaces the older UStaticMeshComponent* Mesh;. In editor builds it can track access and support lazy loading; in a packaged game it compiles down to a plain pointer, so there is no runtime cost. It does not change garbage collection rules: the UPROPERTY is still what keeps the object alive. Use TObjectPtr for reflected members, and plain raw pointers for function parameters and local variables.

short: A pointer to a UObject that does not keep it alive and safely reports null once the object is gone.
long: Sometimes you want to remember an object without claiming it. An enemy can hold a TWeakObjectPtr to its current target: if the target is destroyed, Get() returns nullptr instead of a dangling address, and the enemy does not accidentally keep a dead player in memory. Check IsValid() or Get() before every use. It is ideal for caches, observers, and references held by objects that may outlive what they point at.

short: A reference to an asset by its path, so the asset is only loaded into memory when you ask for it.
long: A hard reference loads the asset whenever the referencing object loads, which can drag huge textures and meshes into memory for no reason. A soft reference stores only the asset's path. A weapon catalog can list fifty weapon meshes as TSoftObjectPtr and load just the one the player equips, either right away with LoadSynchronous or in the background with the streamable manager. TSoftClassPtr does the same for Blueprint classes you plan to spawn.

short: A variable that holds a class rather than an object, limited to one base class and its children.
long: When a tower needs to know what to fire, you do not want an existing fireball; you want the fireball class so it can spawn new ones. UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere) TSubclassOf<ADojoProjectile> ProjectileClass; gives designers a dropdown that only lists projectile classes, including Blueprint children. You then pass it to SpawnActor. This is the clean replacement for hardcoding asset paths in a constructor, which breaks the moment someone renames or moves the Blueprint.

short: A reference-counted smart pointer for ordinary C++ objects that are not UObjects.
long: Garbage collection only covers UObjects. For plain C++ classes, such as a pathfinding result or a parsed save file helper, Unreal offers its own smart pointers. A TSharedPtr counts how many owners an object has and deletes it when the last one lets go. TSharedRef is the never-null version, MakeShared creates one efficiently, and TWeakPtr observes without owning. Never wrap a UObject in a TSharedPtr; the two memory systems fight.

short: A smart pointer that is the single owner of a non-UObject and deletes it automatically when it goes away.
long: A TUniquePtr says: this object has exactly one owner. It cannot be copied, only moved, which makes ownership obvious in the code. When the owning class is destroyed, the object it holds is deleted too, with no manual delete and no leak. It suits private helpers a class fully owns, such as a custom spatial grid inside a manager. Create one with MakeUnique<T>(). Like TSharedPtr, it is not for UObjects.

short: The function that creates a new UObject at runtime that is not an actor or a constructor-made component.
long: Use NewObject when you need a plain UObject during play, such as an inventory item instance or a runtime quest object: UDojoItem* Item = NewObject<UDojoItem>(this);. The first argument is the outer, the object that conceptually owns the new one. NewObject does not keep it alive by itself, so store the result in a UPROPERTY right away. Never use NewObject for actors, which need SpawnActor, and never use C++ new for UObjects.

short: The call that hooks a component made at run time into its world, so it can render, collide, and tick.
long: A component made with CreateDefaultSubobject in a constructor is registered for you when its actor enters the world. A component made later with NewObject is only an object until you call RegisterComponent on it: before that it has no render state, no physics, and no tick. The usual order for a run-time scene component is NewObject with the actor as its outer, SetupAttachment or AttachToComponent to place it, any settings, then RegisterComponent, and AddInstanceComponent if it should show in the Details panel. DestroyComponent unregisters and removes it again.

short: The world function that creates a new actor at runtime at a given location and rotation.
long: Bullets, enemies in a wave, loot drops, and impact effects are all spawned while the game runs. Call GetWorld()->SpawnActor<ADojoProjectile>(ProjectileClass, SpawnLocation, SpawnRotation, SpawnParams); and you get back a pointer to the new actor, or null if spawning failed, for example because of a collision rule. FActorSpawnParameters lets you set the owner, the instigator, and what to do if the spot is blocked. Spawning many actors per second has a cost, which is when an object pool helps.

short: The constructor-only function that creates an actor's built-in components, such as its mesh or collision shape.
long: Components that every instance of a class should have are created in the constructor with CreateDefaultSubobject<UBoxComponent>(TEXT("TriggerBox"));. The name must be unique within the actor and stays stable, because saved levels and Blueprint children refer to it. Since the constructor builds the class default object, these components become part of the template and appear in the Blueprint Components panel. Calling it outside a constructor is an error; at runtime use NewObject and register the component instead.

short: A check that a UObject pointer is not null and that the object is not already being destroyed.
long: A pointer can be non-null and still point at an actor that was destroyed this frame and is waiting for cleanup. IsValid(Target) catches both cases in one call, which makes it safer than comparing against nullptr. Use it before touching any pointer you did not just create, especially cached targets, overlap results, and anything another system could have destroyed. A failed check is a normal game event, so handle it quietly rather than crashing.

short: The function the engine calls once on an actor or component when gameplay starts for it.
long: BeginPlay is where runtime setup goes: caching a pointer to the game mode, binding to an overlap event, starting a timer, or copying max health into current health. By this point the actor is in a world and its components exist. Always call Super::BeginPlay() first so the parent class runs its own setup, which is also what fires the Blueprint BeginPlay event. Constructor for defaults, BeginPlay for gameplay is a rule worth memorizing.

short: The function called when an actor leaves play, whether it was destroyed, the level unloaded, or the game quit.
long: EndPlay is the cleanup counterpart to BeginPlay. Clear timers you started, unbind from delegates on other objects, and release anything you registered with a manager. The EEndPlayReason parameter tells you why: Destroyed, LevelTransition, EndPlayInEditor, Quit, and so on, so a quest giver might save progress only on a level transition. Call Super::EndPlay(EndPlayReason) so parent classes clean up as well.

short: The function the engine calls on an actor or component every frame, if ticking is enabled.
long: Tick(float DeltaTime) is the per-frame update: moving a homing missile, counting down a cooldown, or smoothing a health bar. It is easy to overuse. Something that only needs to happen every half second should use a timer or a tick interval, and something that reacts to an event should use a delegate instead of checking every frame. Turn ticking off entirely for actors that do not need it, because hundreds of idle ticks add up.

short: The number of seconds since the previous frame, passed into Tick so motion and timers stay frame-rate independent.
long: At 60 frames per second DeltaTime is about 0.0167; at 30 it is about 0.033. If you move a projectile by Speed every frame, it flies twice as fast on a fast PC. Move it by Speed * DeltaTime and it covers the same distance per second everywhere. The same applies to cooldowns: subtract DeltaTime from the remaining time each tick. Forgetting DeltaTime is one of the most common causes of gameplay that feels different on different machines.

short: Phases of the frame, before, during, or after physics, that decide when an actor's Tick runs.
long: Not every update should happen at the same moment. Actors tick in the pre-physics group by default, which is right for things that push objects around. A camera that follows a physics-driven ragdoll looks smoother in the post-physics group, because by then the ragdoll has already moved this frame. You set it with PrimaryActorTick.TickGroup or SetTickGroup, and you can also declare that one actor must tick after another with a tick prerequisite.

short: A rule that one actor or component must tick after another within the same frame.
long: Inside one frame the engine calls ticking objects one after another, and their order is not promised by where they sit in the level. When a camera rig must read its pawn's position after the pawn has moved, or a health bar must read health after damage was applied, call AddTickPrerequisiteActor (or AddTickPrerequisiteComponent) so the engine always ticks the dependency first. Tick groups give coarse order around physics; prerequisites give exact order between two things.

short: The thread that runs gameplay: ticking actors and components, Blueprint, input, timers, and delegates.
long: Almost all gameplay code runs on the game thread, which owns every actor and UObject and works through the frame: input, ticks in their tick groups, timers, and delegates. Drawing is prepared on the separate render thread, and some work such as physics or async tasks can run on other threads, but the results come back to the game thread to be read. Code on another thread must not touch actors or UObjects directly; it hands its results to the game thread, and IsInGameThread lets code check where it is running.

short: The thread that turns a frame into draw commands while the game thread works on the next frame, using its own copies of what each component looks like.
long: Gameplay code runs on the game thread. Drawing is prepared on a separate render thread, which can run up to a frame behind. So that the two never fight over the same data, each visible component gives the renderer its own render-side copy, a scene proxy, and sends it updates when something changes. The game thread is then free to move actors for the next frame while the renderer draws the last one from its copies. Game code never touches render-thread data directly; it sends changes across, for example with ENQUEUE_RENDER_COMMAND.

short: The settings struct that controls whether and how often an actor ticks.
long: In the constructor, PrimaryActorTick.bCanEverTick = true; says this class may tick at all; set it to false for actors that never need per-frame work. At runtime, SetActorTickEnabled(false) pauses ticking, for example on a pooled projectile waiting to be reused. SetActorTickInterval(0.5f) makes Tick run twice a second instead of every frame, which is a quick fix for a tower that was firing once per frame. Components have the matching PrimaryComponentTick.

short: A small ID you keep so you can pause, check, or cancel a timer later.
long: Starting a timer gives you nothing to hold unless you pass in a handle. Store it as a member, as in FTimerHandle ReloadTimerHandle;, and you can later ask how much time remains, pause it, or clear it when the player switches weapons. Starting a new timer with the same handle replaces the old one, which is a neat way to restart a cooldown. Clearing timers in EndPlay avoids calls into an object that is going away.

short: A delegate the timer manager can fire, which can carry extra arguments for the function it calls.
long: The simple SetTimer form calls a member function with no arguments. When one object times many things, such as one clock per quest, build an FTimerDelegate with FTimerDelegate::CreateUObject(this, &UTracker::HandleTimeUp, Quest) and pass it to SetTimer; the quest is stored in the delegate as a payload and handed to HandleTimeUp when the timer fires. It is a plain single-cast delegate, so the function needs no UFUNCTION, and a delegate bound with CreateUObject stops firing once its object is destroyed. Keep one FTimerHandle per thing being timed.

short: The world service that calls a function after a delay, or repeatedly at an interval, without using Tick.
long: Timers are the clean answer to do this in 3 seconds or do this every 0.5 seconds. GetWorldTimerManager().SetTimer(FireTimerHandle, this, &ADojoTower::Fire, 0.5f, true); fires the tower twice a second until you call ClearTimer. You can also bind a lambda or set a first delay that differs from the repeat rate. Timers respect game pause and time dilation, and they are cheaper and easier to read than countdown variables in Tick.

short: A type-safe holder for a function to call later, so one object can notify another without knowing its class.
long: A delegate is like leaving your phone number with someone: when the event happens, they call it. A single-cast delegate holds exactly one binding. DECLARE_DELEGATE_OneParam(FOnAmmoChanged, int32) declares the type, BindUObject or BindLambda attaches a function, and ExecuteIfBound calls it safely. Delegates are the engine's form of the observer pattern and the main way to decouple systems, for example letting a HUD react to health changes without the health code knowing the HUD exists.

short: A delegate that can hold many listeners and calls all of them when broadcast.
long: When several systems care about one event, such as a bounty board, the crowd audio, and the scoreboard all reacting to an arena foe falling, a multicast delegate lets each subscribe independently. Declare it with DECLARE_MULTICAST_DELEGATE_OneParam, subscribe with AddUObject or AddLambda, which return a handle you can use to unsubscribe, and fire it with Broadcast. The non-dynamic version is fast and works only from C++; Blueprints cannot bind to it.

short: A delegate that binds by function name through reflection, so it can be saved and used from Blueprints.
long: Dynamic delegates trade a bit of speed for engine integration. Because they look up functions by name, the bound function must be a UFUNCTION, and the delegate can be stored in properties, serialized, and passed as a Blueprint parameter, for example as a callback pin on a node. The macro also needs parameter names, as in DECLARE_DYNAMIC_DELEGATE_OneParam(FOnLoaded, bool, bSuccess). Use the plain version when only C++ needs it.

short: A many-listener delegate that Blueprints can bind to, the C++ version of an event dispatcher.
long: This is the delegate type behind most engine events you bind to, including OnComponentBeginOverlap and OnActorHit. Declare it outside the class, as in DECLARE_DYNAMIC_MULTICAST_DELEGATE_OneParam(FOnHealthChanged, float, NewHealth);, expose an instance with UPROPERTY(BlueprintAssignable), and both C++ (with AddDynamic) and Blueprint graphs (with Bind Event or the event button) can listen. It is the standard bridge for C++ systems that announce events to UI built in Blueprint.

short: The macro that subscribes a UFUNCTION to a dynamic multicast delegate, such as an overlap event.
long: Box->OnComponentBeginOverlap.AddDynamic(this, &ADojoPlate::HandleOverlap); is the line you will write most often for collision. The handler must be a UFUNCTION with exactly the parameter list the delegate expects; if either is wrong, the binding fails at compile time or silently at runtime. Bind in BeginPlay rather than the constructor so the binding is not baked into the class defaults twice. AddUniqueDynamic avoids double binding if the code might run more than once.

short: The call that fires a multicast delegate, invoking every function currently bound to it.
long: OnHealthChanged.Broadcast(CurrentHealth); tells every listener the news in one line. The broadcaster does not know or care who is listening, which is the whole point: you can add a damage number popup later without editing the health component. Broadcasting with no listeners is safe and does nothing. The call order of listeners is not something to depend on, so listeners should not rely on running before or after each other.

short: Removing a listener from a delegate so it stops being called, usually when the listener goes away.
long: Every subscription should have an exit. For dynamic delegates use RemoveDynamic with the same object and function you added; for native multicast delegates keep the FDelegateHandle from AddUObject and pass it to Remove, or call RemoveAll(this). A weapon that subscribes to the owner's fire input should unsubscribe when it is dropped, or the dropped weapon keeps firing. EndPlay is the usual place to unbind from objects that will outlive you.

short: A property specifier that lets Blueprint graphs bind events to a dynamic multicast delegate.
long: Mark a dynamic multicast delegate member with UPROPERTY(BlueprintAssignable) and it shows up in Blueprints as an event you can bind. A game state's OnTimerChanged delegate is a typical case: the HUD widget binds a custom event to it, and whenever C++ broadcasts the new time, the widget updates its text. Without this specifier, only C++ can subscribe.

short: The reflected half of an Unreal interface, which lets unrelated classes promise the same set of functions.
long: A chest, a door, and an NPC have nothing in common in their class trees, yet all can be interacted with. An interface lets each promise an Interact function without sharing a parent. Unreal interfaces come in two parts: a UINTERFACE class prefixed with U that the reflection system sees, and a matching I class that holds the functions you implement. You test for support with Implements<UInteractable>() or by casting to the I type. This keeps the player's interaction code from knowing about every interactable class.

short: The C++ half of an Unreal interface, the I-prefixed class that declares the functions implementers must provide.
long: A class opts into an interface by inheriting from the I class alongside its normal parent, as in class ADojoChest : public AActor, public IInteractable. Functions marked BlueprintNativeEvent or BlueprintImplementableEvent in the interface must be called through the generated static helper, IInteractable::Execute_Interact(Target, Interactor), so that Blueprint implementations work too. Plain C++ interface functions can be called through a cast pointer as usual.

short: A safe conversion of a UObject pointer to a more specific class, returning null if the object is not that class.
long: Engine functions hand you general types: an overlap gives you an AActor*, GetPawn gives you an APawn*. Cast<ADojoPlayer>(OtherActor) checks the real class and returns a typed pointer, or nullptr if it is something else, so always test the result. CastChecked asserts instead of returning null, which is useful when a failure means a bug. Casting is cheap, but code full of casts to specific classes is often a sign an interface or delegate would decouple things better.

short: A check that answers whether an object is a given class or a child of it, without converting the pointer.
long: Other->IsA(ADojoEnemy::StaticClass()) or Other->IsA<ADojoEnemy>() returns true or false. Use it when you only need the yes or no answer, for example to decide which sound to play. When you also need to call functions on the result, Cast is better because it checks and converts in one step. StaticClass() returns the UClass that describes a C++ type, which is also what you pass when a function asks for a class.

short: The actor function that removes an actor from the world; the memory is freed later by garbage collection.
long: Calling Destroy() on a defeated enemy takes it out of play right away: EndPlay runs, it stops ticking and colliding, and other code should treat it as gone. The memory is reclaimed in a later garbage collection pass, which is why other pointers to it should be checked with IsValid. SetLifeSpan(3.f) schedules a destroy for later, handy for shell casings. Functions with a K2_ prefix are Blueprint-facing wrappers; in C++ call Destroy() directly.

short: A function that runs whenever an actor is placed or edited in the editor, and when it is spawned, so it can rebuild itself from its settings.
long: OnConstruction is C++'s version of the Blueprint Construction Script. A fence actor can read its Length property and lay out the right number of fence post meshes, and when a designer drags the length slider the fence updates live in the viewport. Keep it fast and self-contained, because it reruns often while editing. It is not the place for gameplay logic such as finding the player; that belongs in BeginPlay.

short: Unreal's resizable list, the container you will use most for ordered collections.
long: TArray<AActor*> Enemies; holds items in order and grows as needed. Add or Emplace puts items on the end, Remove and RemoveAt take them out, Num tells you how many there are, Contains and Find search, and a range-based for loop walks through them. Marked UPROPERTY, a TArray of UObject pointers keeps those objects alive and shows in the editor. Do not add or remove items while looping over the same array; collect changes and apply them after the loop.

short: A container of key and value pairs with fast lookup by key, like a dictionary.
long: If you keep asking how many of item X the player has, a TMap<FName, int32> answers in one step instead of scanning a list. Add or Emplace inserts, Find returns a pointer to the value or nullptr if the key is missing, FindOrAdd creates a default entry when needed, Contains checks, and Remove deletes. Keys need a hash function, which common types like FName, FString, int32, and UObject pointers already have. Iteration order is not something to depend on.

short: A container of unique values with fast checks for whether a value is present.
long: A TSet is for questions like has this checkpoint been visited or is this actor already in the list. Adding the same value twice keeps one copy. Contains is fast no matter how big the set gets, unlike searching a TArray. A combo system might keep a TSet<FName> of enemies already hit by this swing, so one swing never damages the same enemy twice. Like TMap, the order of items is not guaranteed.

short: A first in, first out container built to be safe for passing items between threads.
long: Items leave a TQueue in the order they arrived: Enqueue adds to the back, Dequeue takes from the front, and IsEmpty checks. It is designed for producer and consumer handoffs, including across threads. It cannot be marked UPROPERTY, so the garbage collector does not see UObject pointers inside it; holding actors that something else already keeps alive is fine, but for gameplay lists such as an object pool, a UPROPERTY TArray is often the simpler, safer pick.

short: Unreal's general-purpose, changeable text string, used for building and manipulating text.
long: FString is the string you edit: join pieces, search, split, or format with FString::Printf(TEXT("Wave %d"), WaveNumber). It is the right type for log messages, file paths, and player-typed input such as a server address. It is not ideal for identifiers you compare often, which is what FName is for, and not for text shown to players, which should be FText so it can be translated. Use the * operator to get a raw character pointer when an API wants one.

short: A lightweight, case-insensitive name used for identifiers like socket names, row names, and tags.
long: Behind the scenes, every FName is stored once in a global table, and the FName itself is just a small index. That makes copying and comparing two FNames as fast as comparing two numbers. Socket names such as hand_r, data table row names, and map keys are typical uses. FNames are not meant to be edited or shown to players. Create one with FName(TEXT("hand_r")), and remember that comparison ignores letter case.

short: The string type for anything players read, built so it can be translated into other languages.
long: Button labels, item descriptions, and dialogue should be FText. It carries the information the localization tools need to swap English for French without code changes, and it formats numbers and dates the way each region expects. Create translatable literals with LOCTEXT or NSLOCTEXT, and wrap dynamic values with FText::FromString or FText::AsNumber. UMG text widgets take FText, so health numbers on a HUD usually end up as FText::AsNumber.

short: A macro that turns a string literal into Unreal's wide character type so it works the same on every platform.
long: Write TEXT("Hello") instead of "Hello" whenever an engine function expects text. The macro makes the literal use TCHAR, the character type the engine is built on, which avoids encoding mix-ups across platforms. It does not make the text translatable by itself; that is the job of FText with LOCTEXT. You will mostly see it in UE_LOG messages, component names in CreateDefaultSubobject, and FString or FName construction.

short: A struct of three numbers, X, Y, and Z, used for positions, directions, velocities, and scale.
long: FVector is the most common math type in the engine. GetActorLocation returns one, velocity is one, and a direction is one with length 1. Useful tools: FVector::Dist for distance, Size and Size2D for length, GetSafeNormal to get a direction, DotProduct to tell whether something is in front of you, and CrossProduct for a perpendicular. In UE5 the components are doubles, which supports very large worlds. A projectile step is Location + Direction * Speed * DeltaTime.

short: A rotation expressed as Pitch, Yaw, and Roll angles in degrees.
long: FRotator is the human-friendly rotation type. Pitch tilts up and down around the Y axis, Yaw turns left and right around the vertical Z axis, and Roll tips side to side around the X axis. Note the constructor order is Pitch, Yaw, Roll, so FRotator(0.f, 90.f, 0.f) is a quarter turn to the right. A rotator can rotate a vector with RotateVector, and turns into a forward direction with Vector(). For combining many rotations, convert to FQuat to avoid gimbal lock.

short: A rotation stored as a quaternion, which combines and blends rotations without the glitches angles can have.
long: You rarely write quaternion math by hand, but the engine uses FQuat internally because it never suffers gimbal lock, where two rotation axes line up and you lose a degree of freedom. It also interpolates smoothly between two orientations. FQuat::Identity means no rotation, which is a neat way to reset a dropped weapon to sit upright. Convert with FQuat(SomeRotator) and SomeQuat.Rotator().

short: A bundle of location, rotation, and scale that describes where something is and how it is oriented and sized.
long: Every scene component has a transform relative to its parent, and every actor has one in world space through its root. FTransform holds a translation vector, a quaternion rotation, and a scale vector. You can convert points between spaces with TransformPosition and InverseTransformPosition, for example to find where a muzzle socket is in the world. Spawning an actor at a transform is a common shortcut instead of passing location and rotation separately.

short: A collection of static math helpers such as clamping, interpolation, random numbers, and trigonometry.
long: FMath is the toolbox you reach for constantly. FMath::Clamp(Health, 0.f, MaxHealth) keeps health in range, FMath::Lerp blends between two values, FMath::FInterpTo eases a value toward a target over time for smooth health bars, FMath::RandRange picks random loot, and IsNearlyEqual compares floats safely. A health bar fill is FMath::Clamp(Current / Max, 0.f, 1.f), which never overflows the bar even if damage overshoots.

short: A class of static math functions written for Blueprints that C++ can call too, such as FindLookAtRotation.
long: Many Blueprint math nodes live in UKismetMathLibrary, and nothing stops C++ from calling them. The most popular is FindLookAtRotation(Start, Target), which returns the rotator that points from one location toward another, perfect for aiming a turret's fireball at the player. Kismet is the old name for Blueprint scripting, which is why the name looks odd. For hot code paths, the FMath and FVector equivalents are usually slightly leaner.

short: A struct describing a collision or trace hit: what was hit, where, and from which direction.
long: Traces, sweeps, and hit events fill an FHitResult for you. GetActor() and GetComponent() say what you hit, ImpactPoint is the exact spot on the surface, ImpactNormal points straight out of that surface, Distance says how far along the trace, and BoneName tells you which bone of a skeletal mesh was struck. A bullet decal goes at ImpactPoint, rotated to face along ImpactNormal; a headshot check compares BoneName to the head bone.

short: A category that collision objects belong to or that a trace tests against, such as Pawn, WorldStatic, or Visibility.
long: Every collidable component has an object type, like Pawn, WorldStatic, WorldDynamic, or PhysicsBody, and a response to every channel. Traces use trace channels such as Visibility and Camera. You can add your own in Project Settings under Collision, for example a Projectile object channel or an Interact trace channel, which appear in code as ECC_GameTraceChannel1 and onward. Channels let you say things like bullets hit pawns and walls but pass through trigger volumes.

short: How a component reacts to a given channel: Ignore it, Overlap it, or Block it.
long: Each component lists a response for every channel. Block stops movement and can fire hit events, Overlap lets things pass through but can fire overlap events, and Ignore pretends the other thing does not exist. When two components meet, the weaker of their two responses wins: if a wall blocks pawns but the pawn ignores the wall, they ignore each other. That rule explains most it does not collide mysteries. Set responses in the Details panel or with SetCollisionResponseToChannel.

short: A named, reusable bundle of collision settings, such as BlockAll, OverlapAllDynamic, Pawn, or NoCollision.
long: Instead of ticking dozens of response boxes per component, you pick a preset, which sets the object type, whether collision is on, and every response at once. NoCollision turns collision off, BlockAll and BlockAllDynamic block everything as a WorldStatic or a WorldDynamic object, OverlapAllDynamic is a query-only WorldDynamic that overlaps everything (every box, sphere, and capsule starts with it), Pawn is set up for character capsules, and Custom lets you set each response by hand. Read a preset's whole table before trusting its name: OverlapOnlyPawn overlaps pawns but leaves most other channels at Block. You can define your own presets in Project Settings.

short: The per-component switches that must be on before overlap events, or physics hit events, will fire.
long: Setting responses to Overlap is not enough on its own. Both components involved must also have Generate Overlap Events enabled, or nothing fires. Physics-driven hits have a similar switch, Simulation Generates Hit Events. These flags exist because events cost time, so the engine lets you turn them off for the thousands of rocks that never need them. If an overlap handler never runs, check these flags on both sides first.

short: An event fired when one component starts or stops intersecting another that is set to overlap it.
long: Overlaps are for areas you pass through: a pickup radius, a door trigger, a damage zone. Begin overlap fires on entry, end overlap on exit. Component versions, such as OnComponentBeginOverlap, tell you exactly which shape was touched, while actor versions fire for any component of the actor. The component handler has a fixed signature: the overlapped component, the other actor, the other component, the body index, a from-sweep flag, and the sweep FHitResult. Bind it with AddDynamic in BeginPlay.

short: An event fired when a moving component runs into something that blocks it.
long: Hits are for solid contact: a projectile striking a wall, a car crashing into a barrier. OnComponentHit gives you the component that was hit, the other actor and component, the impulse, and an FHitResult with the impact point and normal. A move made with a sweep fires a hit on the mover and on the shape it ran into whenever it is stopped, with no extra switch and with a zero impulse; bodies moved by the physics simulation also need Simulation Generates Hit Events turned on, and only they report a real impulse. A pressure plate that should not block players belongs on overlaps instead.

short: Shooting an invisible ray between two points to find what it hits first, or everything it passes through.
long: Traces answer questions like what is under the crosshair or is there a wall between the guard and the player. GetWorld()->LineTraceSingleByChannel(Hit, Start, End, ECC_Visibility, Params) returns true and fills Hit if anything blocking the Visibility channel lies on the line. By-object-type versions test against object types like Pawn, and multi versions return every hit. Pair traces with DrawDebugLine while developing so you can see them. Fast projectiles often trace from last frame's position to this frame's to avoid skipping thin targets.

short: Moving a shape, such as a sphere or box, along a path and reporting what it would hit.
long: A sweep is a line trace with thickness. SweepSingleByChannel with FCollisionShape::MakeSphere(40.f) checks whether a sword arc of that width would connect, which is far more forgiving than a thin ray. Movement can sweep too: SetActorLocation with the sweep flag stops at the first blocking hit instead of teleporting into a wall. Melee hit detection, ledge checks, and making sure a spawn point is clear are common uses.

short: Option structs passed to traces and sweeps to fine-tune them, such as which actors to ignore.
long: Without extra options, a gun's trace starting inside the player will happily hit the player. FCollisionQueryParams Params; Params.AddIgnoredActor(this); fixes that, and also lets you request complex collision or a trace tag for debugging. FCollisionObjectQueryParams says which object types a by-object trace should look for, for example only ECC_Pawn so a fireball's trace ignores scenery. Build these once per call; they are cheap.

short: The per-shape switch that says whether a shape takes part in queries, in physics, in both, or in neither.
long: Collision Enabled is the first of a shape's three collision settings, before its object type and its responses. NoCollision takes part in nothing; QueryOnly answers sweeps, traces, and overlap checks but never pushes or is pushed, which suits triggers; PhysicsOnly lets simulated bodies push it without being found by queries; QueryAndPhysics does both, for solid things. SetCollisionEnabled changes it while the game runs, which is how a breakable wall stops being solid: its overlaps end and swept movers pass through. It is a different tool from changing one response, which lets one kind of thing through and keeps stopping the rest.

short: Asks a shape which actors are overlapping it right now, instead of waiting for an overlap event.
long: Overlap events tell you the moment something arrives or leaves; GetOverlappingActors answers what is there now. It fills a TArray of actors from the list the shape keeps of its current overlaps, optionally filtered to one class, and GetOverlappingComponents does the same for the other shapes. IsOverlappingActor and IsOverlappingComponent check one candidate. They read the same list the events maintain, so they also need Generate Overlap Events on both sides. Use them when a decision depends on the present, such as a gate checking its doorway before it shuts.

short: Letting the physics engine move a component with gravity, forces, and collisions instead of moving it yourself.
long: Turn on Simulate Physics for a primitive component and the Chaos physics engine takes over: crates tumble, barrels roll, ragdolls collapse. You influence simulated bodies with AddImpulse for a one-off shove, like an explosion, or AddForce for a steady push, like wind, scaled by mass. Skeletal meshes use a physics asset, a set of simple bodies per bone, to ragdoll. A simulated component detaches from its parent's movement, so mixing manual movement and simulation on the same component causes fights.

short: A project setting that splits one long frame into several smaller physics steps, so simulated bodies stay stable when the frame rate drops.
long: A spring, a ragdoll, or a stack of crates is tuned for small physics updates; one long frame can make them jitter or fly apart. With substepping turned on in Project Settings under Physics, the engine runs several shorter physics steps inside that frame instead of one long one, up to a maximum count you set. It is the engine's built-in answer for simulated bodies. Gameplay code that must repeat exactly, such as a replay, still needs its own fixed step, because substepping keeps physics stable without making it identical across machines.

short: UE5's input system, where you define abstract actions as assets and map keys to them through mapping contexts.
long: Instead of asking was the space bar pressed, your code asks did the Jump action trigger. Actions are assets, mapping contexts decide which keys, buttons, or sticks drive them, triggers decide when they count, and modifiers reshape the raw values. Swapping to a vehicle can be as simple as removing the on-foot context and adding the driving one. Add EnhancedInput to your module's dependencies in Build.cs before using its classes in C++. It replaced the older action and axis mappings as the default in UE 5.1.

short: An asset that names one thing the player can do, like Jump, Move, or Interact, and the type of value it produces.
long: An input action is a verb, not a key. IA_Move produces a 2D axis value, IA_Jump produces a simple bool, IA_Zoom might produce a 1D axis. Because the action does not know which key drives it, the same IA_Interact works on keyboard, gamepad, and touch. In C++ you hold a pointer to the asset in a UPROPERTY so a designer can assign it, then bind a handler to it through the Enhanced Input component.

short: An asset that maps physical keys and buttons to input actions, and can be switched on and off as a set.
long: A mapping context says W, A, S, D and the left stick drive IA_Move; Space and the bottom face button drive IA_Jump. You activate it for a local player through the Enhanced Input local player subsystem with AddMappingContext(Context, Priority), usually in BeginPlay of the player controller or pawn. Higher priority contexts win conflicts, so a menu context can temporarily claim keys that gameplay also uses, and removing it hands them back.

short: A rule on a mapping or action that decides when input counts, such as on press, on release, after a hold, or on a quick tap.
long: Triggers turn raw button state into intent. With no trigger, an action fires every frame the key is down. Pressed fires once on the way down, Released once on the way up, Hold fires after the key is held for a set time, Tap fires only for a quick press and release, and Chorded requires another action to be active, like a modifier key. A charged heavy attack might use Hold with a one-second threshold while the light attack on the same button uses Tap.

short: A step that reshapes raw input values before they reach your code, like flipping, scaling, or ignoring small stick drift.
long: Modifiers let one action collect input from many keys that each mean something slightly different. For IA_Move, D can pass X as is, A can use Negate so it becomes negative X, and W can use Swizzle to move its value onto the Y axis. Dead Zone ignores tiny thumbstick wobble and Scalar adjusts sensitivity. Done right, your handler just reads one clean 2D vector no matter which device the player uses.

short: The enum you bind against that picks which phase of an action calls your handler: Started, Ongoing, Triggered, Completed, or Canceled.
long: When you bind, you choose a moment. Started fires on the first frame of input, Triggered fires when the triggers are satisfied, which may be every frame for movement, Ongoing fires while a trigger like Hold is still charging, Completed fires when it finishes, and Canceled fires when input stops before a trigger succeeds. A sprint could bind Started to speed up and Completed to slow down, while movement binds Triggered.

short: The value an input action hands to your handler, read as a bool, a float, or a 2D or 3D vector.
long: Handlers bound to Enhanced Input usually take const FInputActionValue& Value. You read it as the type the action was set up for: Value.Get<bool>() for a button, Value.Get<float>() for a trigger or wheel, Value.Get<FVector2D>() for a stick or WASD movement. Reading the wrong type returns a converted value that may not be what you expect, so match the action's value type.

short: The input component used with Enhanced Input, where you bind input actions to handler functions.
long: In SetupPlayerInputComponent, cast the incoming component with CastChecked<UEnhancedInputComponent>(PlayerInputComponent), then call BindAction(MoveAction, ETriggerEvent::Triggered, this, &ADojoHero::Move);. Each binding ties one action and one trigger event to one function. If the cast fails, the project's default input component class is not set to the enhanced one, which is a quick thing to check in Project Settings under Input.

short: The older input setup with Action and Axis Mappings in Project Settings, replaced by Enhanced Input in UE5.
long: Before Enhanced Input, you named actions like Attack in Project Settings, listed the keys for each, and bound them in code with InputComponent->BindAction("Attack", IE_Pressed, this, &AMyController::OnAttack);. Many tutorials and books written for UE4 and early UE5 still use it. It is deprecated, so new UE5 projects should use Enhanced Input, but recognizing the old style helps you read older code and port it.

short: The pawn function the engine calls when a player possesses it, where you bind input actions to handlers.
long: Override SetupPlayerInputComponent on your pawn or character to wire input to behavior. The engine passes in the input component, you bind your actions, and from then on pressing keys calls your functions. Player controllers have a matching SetupInputComponent for input that should work no matter which pawn is controlled, such as opening the pause menu. Call the Super version first so parent bindings still apply.

short: An asset made from a C++ class whose only job is to hold configuration data designers can edit.
long: Make a class like UDojoWeaponData : public UDataAsset with UPROPERTY fields for damage, fire rate, and mesh, and designers can create as many weapon data assets in the Content Browser as they like. Gameplay code then reads from whichever asset it is given. This separates numbers from logic, so balancing a weapon never means editing a Blueprint graph.

short: A data asset the Asset Manager can find, list, and load by ID, which helps with large or streamed content.
long: UPrimaryDataAsset adds an identity the Asset Manager understands. With that, you can ask for every item definition of type Weapon without hard-referencing all of them, load only the ones you need, and control what gets packaged. For a small project a plain data asset is fine; once you have hundreds of items or downloadable content, primary data assets plus soft references keep memory and load times under control.

short: A spreadsheet-like asset where every row uses the same struct, often imported from CSV or JSON.
long: Data tables shine when you have many entries with the same shape: fifty enemy types, a hundred dialogue lines, every level's XP threshold. Define a row struct, create a table from it, and fill or import rows. In code, Table->FindRow<FDojoEnemyRow>(RowName, TEXT("Spawner")) returns a pointer to the row or null. Designers can edit everything in a grid, and you can round-trip it through a spreadsheet tool.

short: The base struct that a data table's row type must inherit from.
long: To use a struct as a data table row, write USTRUCT(BlueprintType) struct FDojoEnemyRow : public FTableRowBase and give it UPROPERTY fields like MaxHealth and Speed. The base struct is what lets the editor and the import tools recognize the type as a valid row. Each row is identified by an FName row name, which is the key you pass to FindRow.

short: An asset holding a curve that maps one number to another, such as time to height or level to damage.
long: Curves let designers draw behavior instead of typing formulas. A door's opening motion, a jump pad's launch strength over charge time, or XP needed per level can each be a UCurveFloat, and code reads it with Curve->GetFloatValue(X). Combined with a timeline, a curve drives smooth animated values over time without writing easing math. Changing the feel then means dragging curve keys, not recompiling.

short: The scene component at the top of an actor's component tree, whose transform is the actor's transform.
long: Moving an actor really moves its root component, and every attached child follows. Choosing the root matters: for a pickup or projectile, making the collision shape the root means movement and sweeps use that clean shape. Set it in the constructor with SetRootComponent(TriggerBox) or by assigning RootComponent, then attach the other components below it with SetupAttachment. ACharacter already sets its capsule as the root.

short: Functions that connect a component or actor to a parent so it moves with it, optionally at a socket.
long: Use SetupAttachment in a constructor to build the default tree, and AttachToComponent or AttachToActor at runtime, for example when a hero picks up a sword. The transform rules say what happens to the child's position: SnapToTargetIncludingScale moves it exactly onto the target socket, while KeepWorldTransform leaves it where it is. DetachFromActor with KeepWorldTransform drops the item in place. Passing a socket name attaches to a specific bone point.

short: A named attachment point on a mesh, usually on a bone, where you can attach weapons, effects, or other objects.
long: A socket is like a hook sewn onto a costume. Add one to a skeleton's right-hand bone, nudge its offset in the editor with a preview mesh until the sword grip sits right, and name it hand_rSocket. In code, attach the sword to the character's mesh at that FName, and it follows the hand through every animation. Static meshes can have sockets too, such as a muzzle point on a gun model where projectiles spawn.

short: The C++ class behind an animation blueprint, holding the variables that decide which animation plays.
long: Each skeletal mesh that plays an animation blueprint runs an anim instance. A C++ parent class, such as UDojoAnimInstance with Speed and State properties, gives the blueprint clean variables to read in its state machine. The tidy way to fill them is to override NativeUpdateAnimation and pull values from the owner, found with TryGetPawnOwner, every frame. The character can also push values in, but then the character has to know about its animation class, which couples the two.

short: A special Blueprint that decides, every frame, what pose a skeletal mesh should be in.
long: An animation blueprint has an Event Graph for gathering data and an AnimGraph that blends animations into a final pose. You create it for a specific skeleton and can give it a C++ anim instance as its parent class. Then you assign it on the mesh component by setting the animation mode to use an animation blueprint and choosing it as the Anim Class.
