Enemy and player can share one animation blueprint if they share a skeleton and a parent anim instance.

short: A graph inside an animation blueprint made of states, like Locomotion or Attack, and rules for moving between them.
long: A state machine breaks a character's animation into clear modes. Locomotion blends idle, walk, and run; Attack plays a swing; Hit plays a flinch; Die plays a fall. Arrows between states carry transition rules, small boolean checks such as State equals Attack. Driving the rules from one enum variable on the anim instance keeps everything readable. It is the same state pattern you would use in gameplay code, drawn as a graph.

short: An asset that smoothly blends between animations based on one or two input values, like speed and direction.
long: Rather than snapping from walk to run, a blend space places animations along an axis and mixes the neighbors. A 1D blend space for locomotion might put idle at speed 0, walk at 200, and run at 500, so a character moving at 350 shows a natural mix of walk and run. A 2D version adds direction for strafing. Feed it the character's ground speed from the movement component's velocity.

short: A marker placed on an animation's timeline that fires an event when playback reaches it.
long: Notifies sync gameplay to animation frames. Put one called AttackEnds near the end of a swing, and the animation blueprint receives an AnimNotify_AttackEnds event it can use to return to Locomotion. Others might enable a sword's damage window, play a footstep sound, or spawn dust. Notify states cover a span of frames with begin and end events. You can also write a C++ UAnimNotify subclass so the same notify is reusable across animations.

short: An asset for playing one-off animations like attacks or reloads on top of the normal animation flow, with sections and slots.
long: State machines are great for steady modes; montages are great for actions. A montage wraps one or more animations, can be split into named sections such as combo steps, and plays through a slot node in the animation blueprint, often only on the upper body. Trigger it from C++ with AnimInstance->Montage_Play(AttackMontage) or ACharacter::PlayAnimMontage, and react to its end with montage delegates. Most combat systems use montages for attacks.

short: The base class for a piece of UI built in UMG, such as a HUD, a menu, or a health bar.
long: A user widget is a screen element you design in the Widget Designer and script in Blueprint or C++. A C++ parent class, such as UDojoHealthBar, can hold the logic and pointers to child widgets, while the Widget Blueprint handles layout. Show it with CreateWidget<UDojoHUD>(PlayerController, HUDClass) followed by AddToViewport(), and remove it with RemoveFromParent(). Override NativeConstruct for setup once the widget's children exist.

short: Unreal Motion Graphics, the editor and framework for building game UI out of widgets.
long: UMG gives you a visual designer with panels for layout, such as Canvas, Vertical Box, and Overlay, and controls such as Button, Text, Image, Progress Bar, and Editable Text. Anchors keep elements in the right corner on any screen size. Behavior is wired up in the widget's graph or in a C++ parent class. Add UMG to your Build.cs dependencies before using widget classes from C++.

short: A metadata key that links a C++ widget pointer to a widget with the same name in the Widget Blueprint.
long: Declare UPROPERTY(meta = (BindWidget)) TObjectPtr<UProgressBar> HealthBar; in your C++ widget class, then in the designer add a Progress Bar and name it exactly HealthBar. The engine fills the pointer for you, and the Widget Blueprint will refuse to compile if the named widget is missing, which catches typos early. BindWidgetOptional allows the widget to be absent. This keeps logic in C++ and layout in the designer.

short: A component that shows a UMG widget attached to an actor, like a health bar floating above an enemy.
long: Add a widget component to an enemy, choose the widget class, set its draw size, and pick a space. Screen space keeps it flat and facing the camera at a constant size, which suits name tags and health bars; world space renders it as a panel in the scene, which suits an in-world terminal. Get the live widget with GetUserWidgetObject() and cast it to your widget class to update it.

short: The controller that drives a non-player pawn, moving it with pathfinding and running its decision logic.
long: An AI controller is the computer's version of a player controller. Assign it on the pawn with AIControllerClass and choose when it auto-possesses. It can walk its pawn along the nav mesh with MoveToActor or MoveToLocation, stop with StopMovement, and run a behavior tree with RunBehaviorTree. Simple enemies can make decisions in C++ on the controller; richer ones move that logic into a behavior tree and blackboard.

short: An asset that organizes AI decisions as a tree of tasks, checked from the top down to choose what to do.
long: A behavior tree reads like a priority list. A selector tries its children in order until one succeeds, such as attack if in range, else chase if a target is known, else patrol. A sequence runs children one after another until one fails. Decorators are conditions that gate a branch, services update data on an interval, and tasks are the leaves that actually act. It keeps AI logic visual and easy to rearrange as designs change.

short: The memory a behavior tree reads and writes: named keys such as TargetActor or LastSeenLocation.
long: A blackboard is the AI's notepad. Perception code writes TargetActor when it spots the player, a service writes DistanceToTarget, and the tree's decorators read those keys to pick a branch. Because the tree only talks to keys, you can swap how data is gathered without editing the tree. Keys have types such as Object, Vector, Bool, and Enum, and are defined in a blackboard asset linked to the tree.

short: The generated map of walkable surfaces that AI uses to find paths around obstacles.
long: Drop a Nav Mesh Bounds Volume over your level and the engine builds a nav mesh of the floors a typical agent can walk on. When an AI controller is told to move somewhere, it searches this mesh for a path, using an A star style search, and the pawn follows it. Press P in the editor viewport to see the walkable area in green. If AI refuses to move, the usual causes are no bounds volume, a target off the mesh, or an agent too large for a gap.

short: An older, simple component that lets AI see and hear pawns within a radius and fires events when it does.
long: Pawn sensing gives an enemy a sight radius, a peripheral vision angle, and a hearing threshold, then fires OnSeePawn when a pawn comes into view. It is quick to set up for a first enemy that chases the player. For new work, the AI Perception system is more flexible: it supports more senses, remembers stimuli over time, and works with teams. Both feed the same kind of decision: set a target, then chase.

short: The modern sensing system for AI, with configurable senses like sight, hearing, and damage.
long: An AI perception component on the controller listens for stimuli from configured senses. Sight has a radius and angle, hearing reacts to noise events you report, and damage tells the AI who hurt it. It fires updates when targets are sensed or lost and keeps a memory of each stimulus for a while, so a guard can search the last known location. Pair it with a blackboard so the behavior tree reacts to what the AI knows.

short: The engine automatically copying actors and marked properties from the server to clients.
long: In Unreal multiplayer the server is the source of truth, and replication keeps clients in sync with it. Set bReplicates = true on an actor and the server will create it on clients; turn on Replicate Movement and its position follows too. Individual properties replicate when marked Replicated. Replication only flows from server to clients; clients send their wishes back through server RPCs. Even a single-player game runs on this framework, so thinking about who owns what early saves pain later.

short: A property that the server sends to clients whenever its value changes.
long: Three steps make a property replicate. Mark it UPROPERTY(Replicated), override GetLifetimeReplicatedProps and register it with DOREPLIFETIME(ADojoCharacter, Health) after calling Super, and make sure the actor itself replicates. Include Net/UnrealNetwork.h for the macro. From then on, changing Health on the server updates every client. Change it only on the server; a client-side change is overwritten at the next update and never reaches anyone else.

short: A function that runs on clients when a replicated property's new value arrives.
long: UPROPERTY(ReplicatedUsing = OnRep_Health) float Health; tells the engine to call OnRep_Health on each client after Health changes, which is the perfect place to update a health bar or play a hurt flash. The function must be a UFUNCTION. In C++ the notify does not run on the server automatically, so a listen server host that also needs the visual update should call the same function after changing the value. RepNotify suits lasting state better than a multicast RPC does.

short: Whether this machine's copy of an actor is the official one that is allowed to change game state.
long: For actors spawned by the server, the server's copy has authority and clients have proxies. HasAuthority() returns true on the authoritative copy, so damage, scoring, and spawning belong inside an if (HasAuthority()) check. The local role adds detail: an autonomous proxy is the client's own controlled pawn, while simulated proxies are everyone else's. Most beginner multiplayer bugs come from running authoritative logic on a client.

short: Which networking role the whole running game has: standalone, listen server, dedicated server, or client.
long: GetNetMode() tells you what kind of process you are in. Standalone is offline single-player, a listen server is a host who also plays, a dedicated server runs with no local player, and a client is connected to a server. It answers a different question from authority, which is per actor. A defense tower can use GetNetMode() != NM_Client to make sure only the server spawns its projectiles.

short: A game that acts as the server while one of the players also plays on it.
long: With a listen server, one player hosts and others join their machine. It is cheap, needs no separate server, and suits co-op and casual games. The host has authority and no lag, which can feel unfair in competitive games. You can start one by opening a level with the listen option, for example OpenLevel with the options string ?listen, or by choosing Play As Listen Server in the editor's play settings.

short: A server build that runs the game with no local player, rendering, or input, only simulation.
long: Competitive and large-scale games run dedicated servers in data centers so no player has a host advantage. A dedicated server is a separate build target with no graphics, which makes it lighter, and you test it in the editor by choosing Play As Client, which starts a hidden server behind the scenes. Code that touches UI or local players must not assume they exist on this kind of server.

short: A function that loads a different level, optionally with options such as hosting or joining a game.
long: UGameplayStatics::OpenLevel(this, FName("Arena")) unloads the current map and loads Arena, which is how a main menu starts a match. Adding the options string ?listen makes the new level a listen server, and passing an IP address as the level name joins a server at that address. Because the current world is torn down, only things like the game instance and its subsystems survive the trip.

short: The macro that writes a message to the Output Log and log file, with a category and a severity.
long: UE_LOG(LogTemp, Warning, TEXT("Health dropped to %f"), Health); prints a yellow line in the Output Log and saves it in the project's Saved/Logs folder. The verbosity, such as Error, Warning, Display, Log, or Verbose, sets the color and lets you filter noise. The format works like printf, so FStrings need the * operator. LogTemp is fine for quick checks; real systems deserve their own log category so you can filter just that system.

short: A named channel for log messages, such as LogDojoCombat, so you can filter and control one system's output.
long: Declare a category in a header with DECLARE_LOG_CATEGORY_EXTERN(LogDojoCombat, Log, All); and define it once in a .cpp with DEFINE_LOG_CATEGORY(LogDojoCombat);. Then UE_LOG(LogDojoCombat, Verbose, ...) lines can be filtered in the Output Log or turned up and down at runtime with a console command, without touching other systems' logs. For a category used in only one file, DEFINE_LOG_CATEGORY_STATIC does both steps at once.

short: A function that prints a temporary colored message directly on the game screen.
long: GEngine->AddOnScreenDebugMessage(-1, 2.f, FColor::Cyan, TEXT("Hit enemy")); shows text over the game for two seconds, the C++ twin of Blueprint's Print String. Passing a fixed key instead of -1 replaces the previous message with that key, which is handy for a live readout like current speed. Check that GEngine is not null first, and remove these calls before shipping or wrap them in a debug flag.

short: An assertion that stops the program immediately if a condition you swear is always true turns out false.
long: check(HealthComponent != nullptr); documents an assumption and enforces it: if it ever fails, the editor or game halts and points at the line, so you find the bug at its source instead of three systems later. checkf adds a formatted message. Use check only for programmer mistakes that make continuing pointless. It is compiled out of shipping builds by default, so never put needed work inside it; verify keeps the expression in shipping.

short: A soft assertion that reports a failed condition with a callstack but lets the game keep running.
long: ensure is for things that should not happen but are survivable. if (!ensure(WeaponData)) { return; } logs a loud error with a callstack the first time it fails, breaks into the debugger if attached, then lets you bail out gracefully. That makes it friendlier than check during development of content-driven code, where a designer forgetting to assign an asset should not crash the editor. ensureMsgf adds a message, and ensureAlways reports every time instead of once.

short: Recompiling C++ while the editor is open and patching the changes into the running editor.
long: Press the Compile button in the editor's status bar, or Ctrl+Alt+F11, and Live Coding rebuilds your changed code and swaps it into the running editor, often in seconds. It handles changes inside function bodies very well. Changes to class layouts, such as adding a UPROPERTY, a UFUNCTION, or a new class, are riskier and may need you to close the editor and do a full build from your IDE. It replaced the older Hot Reload feature.

short: The program that reads your module and target files and builds the C++ for a chosen platform and configuration.
long: When you press Build in your IDE, the IDE actually runs the Unreal Build Tool. It reads every Build.cs and Target.cs file, runs the header tool, works out include paths and dependencies, and calls the compiler for the platform you chose. It also generates IDE project files. When a build error mentions a missing module or an unresolved external symbol, the fix is often a dependency line in Build.cs that this tool reads.

short: A C# file per module that tells the build tool what other modules your code depends on.
long: Every module has a file like DojoGame.Build.cs. The most edited lines list dependencies, for example PublicDependencyModuleNames.AddRange(new string[] { "Core", "CoreUObject", "Engine", "InputCore", "EnhancedInput", "UMG" });. If you include a header from a module that is not listed, you will get include or linker errors. Public dependencies are exposed to modules that depend on yours; private ones stay internal and keep build times down.

short: A self-contained unit of C++ code with its own Build.cs, compiled into its own library.
long: The engine itself is hundreds of modules, such as Core, Engine, and AIModule, and your game is at least one more. Each module has a folder under Source, a Build.cs file, and a small file that registers it, which for the main game module uses IMPLEMENT_PRIMARY_GAME_MODULE. Splitting code into modules, for example a separate editor-only tools module, keeps dependencies clean and speeds up builds when one area changes.

short: A C# file that describes one kind of executable to build, such as the game, the editor, or a server.
long: A project usually has DojoGame.Target.cs for the packaged game and DojoGameEditor.Target.cs for the editor build, and can add Server or Client targets for multiplayer. Each sets a TargetType and lists the modules to include. You rarely edit these early on, but knowing they exist explains why your IDE offers both Development and Development Editor configurations.

short: The small JSON file at the root of a project that names the engine version, the modules, and the enabled plugins.
long: Double-clicking a .uproject opens the project in the editor. Inside it is readable JSON: which engine version it is associated with, which C++ modules to load and when, and which plugins are on, such as EnhancedInput or GameplayAbilities. Right-clicking it in the file explorer gives options like Generate Visual Studio project files and Switch Unreal Engine version. Keep it in source control; it is small and essential.

short: A macro like DOJOGAME_API on a class that exports it so other modules can use it.
long: When you create a class through the editor wizard, it writes class DOJOGAME_API ADojoDoor : public AActor. The macro marks the class for export from its module's library, which other modules need in order to link against it. Inside a single game module it is harmless to keep, and removing it only matters if another module needs the class. MinimalAPI on a UCLASS exports just enough for casting and type checks.

short: Rebuilding your IDE's solution from the source folders, needed after adding, moving, or deleting C++ files outside the editor.
long: Your IDE solution is generated, not hand-maintained. When you add a class through the editor, it refreshes the solution for you. When you create, rename, or delete .h and .cpp files by hand, right-click the .uproject and choose Generate project files, or use the editor's refresh option, so the IDE and the build tool see the change. Stale project files cause errors that look like missing classes.

short: The optimization and debugging levels you can build with, from DebugGame for stepping through code to Shipping for release.
long: Development Editor is the everyday choice: optimized engine, debuggable game code, editor included. DebugGame turns off optimization for your game code so breakpoints and variable inspection are reliable while the engine stays fast. Development is a standalone game with logs and console commands, and Shipping strips logging, asserts, and the console for the best performance. Bugs that appear only in Shipping often trace back to code inside a check that was compiled out.

short: Running the editor from your IDE so you can pause on breakpoints, step through code, and inspect variables.
long: Launch the editor from your IDE with the debugger attached, using DebugGame Editor or Development Editor, and you can set a breakpoint in a damage function, trigger it in play, and inspect every variable at that moment. You can also attach to an editor that is already running. Close the project from the editor rather than stopping the debugger, so unsaved work and imported assets are not lost.

short: The working split where C++ builds systems and exposes them, and Blueprints configure and script content on top.
long: Neither side should do everything. C++ is best for core systems, performance-sensitive logic, complex algorithms, and anything many classes share; it is also easier to diff and review. Blueprints are best for content: tuning values, wiring one-off level events, cosmetic reactions, and fast iteration by designers. A healthy pattern is a C++ base class with BlueprintCallable functions, BlueprintImplementableEvent hooks, and EditAnywhere properties, plus a Blueprint child per variant that supplies meshes, sounds, and numbers.

short: A Blueprint asset that inherits from your C++ class so designers can set assets and values without code.
long: Write ADojoTower in C++, then in the Content Browser create a Blueprint Class and pick ADojoTower as the parent, naming it BP_Tower. The Blueprint inherits all your components and properties and adds the things C++ should not hardcode: the mesh, the projectile class, the sound. You can make several variants, like BP_Tower_Fast and BP_Tower_Heavy, from one C++ class. If you later change the parent, use File and then Reparent Blueprint.

short: A Blueprint graph that belongs to one level, for scripting events specific to that map.
long: Each level has its own Level Blueprint, handy for map-only moments like opening a gate when a boss dies or showing the lobby menu when the menu map loads. Because it lives inside the map, nothing else can reuse it, and it is hard to find later. Anything you might want in two levels, such as a HUD setup or a match timer, belongs in a reusable actor, the game mode, or the game state instead.

short: Running the game inside the editor, with options for several players and different network setups.
long: Press Play and the editor creates a separate play world from your level, so changes made while playing are thrown away when you stop. The play options let you choose the number of players and a net mode, such as Play As Listen Server, which opens extra windows as clients so you can test multiplayer on one machine. Simulate runs the world without possessing a pawn, which is useful for watching AI.

short: A UObject subclass whose UPROPERTY fields get written to disk and read back to save player progress.
long: Make UDojoSaveGame : public USaveGame with UPROPERTY fields such as unlocked levels and best times. To save, create one with UGameplayStatics::CreateSaveGameObject, fill it, and call SaveGameToSlot with a slot name and user index. To load, check DoesSaveGameExist and call LoadGameFromSlot, then cast. Async versions avoid hitches. Saving actor pointers does not work across sessions; save stable IDs, like an FName or a gameplay tag, and look things up again on load.

short: Hierarchical labels like Status.Stunned or Damage.Fire that you define once and attach to things to describe them.
long: Instead of a growing pile of bools or string comparisons, gameplay tags give you a shared, typo-proof vocabulary. Tags are defined in project settings or in C++, are grouped by dots, and live in an FGameplayTagContainer on whatever needs them. HasTag answers whether something is stunned, and matching a parent tag such as Damage catches Damage.Fire and Damage.Ice too. They are central to the Gameplay Ability System but useful on their own; add the GameplayTags module to Build.cs.

short: Epic's large plugin framework for abilities, stats, buffs, cooldowns, and their networking.
long: GAS bundles several ideas: abilities are actions like Dash or Fireball, attribute sets hold numbers like Health and Mana, gameplay effects change those numbers or apply tags, and cues play the visuals. An ability system component on an actor ties it together and handles replication and prediction. It is powerful and used in shipped games, but it has a steep learning curve, so build a small ability system by hand first and then study GAS to see the same patterns at scale.

short: A C++ test registered with the engine's automation framework, run from the editor or the command line.
long: IMPLEMENT_SIMPLE_AUTOMATION_TEST(FDojoHealthDamageTest, "Dojo.Health.TakesDamage", flags) declares a test, and its RunTest function sets up objects, calls the code, and checks results with helpers like TestEqual and TestTrue. Wrap tests in #if WITH_DEV_AUTOMATION_TESTS so they never ship. Run them from the Session Frontend's automation tab or headless from the command line, which is how a continuous build can prove a health component still clamps at zero after every change.

short: A class full of static helper functions for common gameplay tasks, usable from C++ and Blueprints.
long: UGameplayStatics is where you find quick answers: GetPlayerController, GetPlayerCharacter, GetGameMode, GetGameState, OpenLevel, PlaySoundAtLocation, SpawnEmitterAtLocation, ApplyDamage, and save game helpers. Most functions take a world context object as the first argument, usually this, so they know which world to act on. They are convenient, but calling GetAllActorsOfClass every frame is slow; cache results or use a registry instead.

short: A global pointer to the running engine object, used for engine-wide services such as on-screen debug messages.
long: GEngine points at the single UEngine instance. Gameplay code mostly touches it for AddOnScreenDebugMessage and for engine subsystems, and it can be null very early in startup, so check it before use. It is a global, which makes it convenient and also easy to overuse; prefer reaching things through the world, the game instance, or a subsystem so dependencies stay visible.

short: Constructor-only helpers that look up an asset or class by its content path.
long: FClassFinder and FObjectFinder let a constructor grab an asset by path, for example a default pawn Blueprint for a game mode. They work, and templates use them, but the path is a hardcoded string: rename or move the asset and the lookup fails, sometimes only in a packaged build. Prefer exposing a TSubclassOf or TObjectPtr property and assigning it in a Blueprint child or the class defaults. Use the helpers only in constructors.

short: A macro that strongly asks the compiler to paste a small function's body at each call site instead of calling it.
long: Tiny getters that return a member, such as FORCEINLINE UCameraComponent* GetCamera() const { return Camera; }, are typical candidates. Inlining removes the cost of a function call, which matters only in very hot code, and modern compilers already inline small functions on their own. Use it for trivial one-liners in headers; putting it on large functions bloats the code. Marking such getters const is a good habit.

short: Telling the compiler a class exists without including its header, so headers stay light and builds stay fast.
long: If your header only stores a pointer to a camera component, write class UCameraComponent; near the top instead of including its header, and include the real header in the .cpp where you actually call its functions. This cuts the chain of headers every other file must parse, which noticeably speeds up builds in big projects, and avoids circular includes between two classes that reference each other.

short: An alias for the parent class, used to call the parent's version of a function you have overridden.
long: Unreal's reflection gives every class a Super typedef for its direct parent. When you override BeginPlay, Tick, EndPlay, or SetupPlayerInputComponent, call Super::BeginPlay() and so on so the parent's work still happens; skipping it can silently break Blueprint events, ticking, or input. Mark the override with the override keyword so the compiler catches signature typos.

short: Reusing a set of already spawned actors instead of spawning and destroying them over and over.
long: A tower that fires ten fireballs a second spawns and destroys hundreds of actors a minute, which costs time and creates garbage collection work. A pool keeps inactive fireballs around: to fire, take one from the pool, reset it, and show it; when it hits or expires, hide it, turn off its collision and ticking, and put it back. Store the pool in a UPROPERTY TArray so the collector knows about it, and give pooled actors a clear Reset function.

short: A text command typed into the in-game console, with the tilde key, to inspect or change the running game.
long: Press the tilde key and type stat fps to see frame rate, stat unit to see where frame time goes, or r.SetRes 1280x720w to resize the window. Console variables, often called CVars, are settings you can read and change this way, and you can define your own for debug toggles. From C++, APlayerController::ConsoleCommand runs a command programmatically. Console access is stripped from Shipping builds by default.

short: Measuring where frame time and memory go so you optimize the real bottleneck instead of guessing.
long: Start broad with stat unit, which splits frame time into game thread, render thread, and GPU, so you know which side is slow. Then dig deeper: Unreal Insights records detailed timing and memory traces you can scrub through, and the GPU Visualizer breaks down rendering cost. View modes like shader complexity reveal expensive materials. Profile in a Development build rather than the editor when you can, since the editor adds its own overhead.

short: Turning the project into a standalone game build that runs without the editor.
long: Packaging compiles the game target, cooks content into platform-ready formats, and bundles everything into an output folder with an executable. Before packaging, set Maps and Modes, such as the default game mode and the map the game starts on, and list every map that must be included, because maps loaded only by name might otherwise be left out. Pick the configuration: Development for testing with a console, Shipping for release.

short: Epic's style rules for Unreal C++, including the type prefixes A, U, F, E, I, T, and b for booleans.
long: The prefixes carry meaning the tools rely on: A for actors, U for other UObjects, F for structs and plain classes, E for enums, I for interfaces, T for templates, and b for bool variables such as bIsDead. Leaving off a prefix on a reflected class causes header tool errors. The standard also covers braces on their own lines, PascalCase names, and preferring engine containers. Following it makes your code read like the engine's own, which helps every reader.

short: A controller taking control of a pawn, so the controller's input or AI decisions drive that pawn.
long: Controller->Possess(Pawn) links mind and body. Player controllers usually possess the default pawn at spawn; AI controllers possess a pawn when it is placed or spawned, depending on its AutoPossessAI setting. OnPossess is a good hook for setup that needs both, such as adding an input mapping context. GetPawn on the controller and GetController on the pawn walk the link in either direction, and you will usually cast the result to your own class.

short: The game mode setting that picks which pawn class each player spawns as, alongside the other framework class choices.
long: A game mode lists the classes the framework should create: DefaultPawnClass for the player's body, PlayerControllerClass, GameStateClass, PlayerStateClass, and HUDClass. Set them in a Blueprint child of your game mode or in the C++ constructor, and choose the game mode per project in Maps and Modes or per level in World Settings. If your new character never appears when you press Play, this is the first setting to check.

short: An editor helper that groups object changes into one undoable step for the editor's undo history.
long: Editor tools and Details panel edits become undoable by opening an FScopedTransaction for the duration of the change and calling Modify() on each object before changing it. Modify records the object's state, so undo can restore it, and everything changed inside one transaction undoes as one step. It works on whole object states, much like a snapshot, and only in the editor; it is not a gameplay undo system.

short: A helper that runs the same small function for a range of indices, sharing them between the engine's worker threads and the calling thread, and returns only when every index is done.
long: ParallelFor(Count, Body) calls Body once for each index from 0 to Count minus 1. The calls are shared between worker threads and the thread that called ParallelFor, which also runs some of them and then waits until every one has finished, so nothing the body did is still in flight when ParallelFor returns. It suits independent work such as filling an array or counting per item. Because some calls run on worker threads, the body must not touch actors or UObjects; it writes only its own slot of an array or hands results to a thread-safe queue such as a TQueue in multi-producer mode.

short: A design where an object is always in exactly one of a fixed set of modes, and each mode decides how the object answers each input.
long: A finite state machine has a fixed list of modes, exactly one current mode, inputs that arrive one at a time, and for each mode a set of rules saying which inputs move it to which other mode. Inputs a mode has no rule for are ignored. In Unreal gameplay code it is usually a UENUM with a switch per input, or one UObject class per mode; the character movement component's movement modes and StateTree assets are engine examples. It is different from the Animation Blueprint state machine, which chooses poses.

short: An engine plugin for data-driven, hierarchical state machines: states arranged in a tree, each with tasks and transitions, edited as an asset.
long: StateTree lets you build a state machine as an asset in the editor. States sit in a tree, so a parent state can hold rules its children share; each state runs tasks while it is active, and transitions with conditions move between states, triggered by task results, conditions, or events sent from C++ with UStateTreeComponent's SendStateTreeEvent. A StateTree component on an actor or AI controller runs it. It suits AI and gameplay flows a designer wants to rearrange and debug visually, with C++ supplying the actions.

short: A class specifier that marks a class as a parent only, so it cannot be placed in a level or spawned on its own.
long: Put Abstract in a class's UCLASS specifiers when the class exists to be derived from, such as a trap base or an ability base. The editor will not let a designer drag it into a level, spawning it fails, and Blueprint children of it work normally. Pair it with a pure virtual or native-event hook that every child must fill in, so only complete kinds of the family ever exist in the game.

short: Objects created and tuned right inside another object's Details panel, owned by it and saved with it.
long: Mark a UObject class EditInlineNew and a pointer property to it Instanced, and the Details panel stops offering a picker for existing objects: it offers a dropdown of classes, creates a new object whose outer is the owner, and shows that object's settings inline. The new object is saved in the owner's file and copied when the owner is duplicated, which makes it a good home for small configurable pieces such as the effects listed in an ability asset. DefaultToInstanced on the class makes every property of its type instanced, the way components behave. Because an asset is shared by everyone who loads it, the objects inside it are shared as well, so they should hold settings and keep no state that changes while the game runs.

short: Function metadata that lets a Blueprint call the function only on itself, so a base class's tools stay inside its own family.
long: A BlueprintCallable function with meta = (BlueprintProtected) shows up for Blueprint children of the class, where they can call it on themselves, but other Blueprints cannot call it on someone else. It is the Blueprint counterpart of a C++ protected function, and suits the tools a base class offers its subclasses, such as taking an item from a visitor or hurting fighters in a radius.

short: A loop helper that visits every actor of a class in a world.
long: for (TActorIterator<AMyActor> It(GetWorld()); It; ++It) walks every actor of that class, and its children, in the given world. It is handy for a base class tool such as finding every fighter in range, but it visits every actor of the class each time, so for frequent per-frame searches a tracked list or an overlap query is cheaper. It lives in EngineUtils.h.

short: Asks an actor for the first component of a given class it carries, or nullptr when it has none.
long: Code that has an actor and needs one of its abilities asks for the part instead of casting the actor: Actor->FindComponentByClass<UHealthComponent>() returns that actor's health component whatever kind of actor it is. It searches the actor's component list each call, so code that asks often can keep the result. GetComponentByClass does the same, and has a Blueprint node, Get Component by Class.

short: A class of static functions that C++ and every Blueprint graph can call, with no object to create first.
long: Derive from UBlueprintFunctionLibrary and mark static functions BlueprintCallable or BlueprintPure, and they appear as nodes in every graph. It suits helpers that belong to no single actor, such as assembling a kind of prop from parts or formatting a score. The engine's own Gameplay Statics and Kismet Math Library are function libraries.

short: A component's startup step that runs after it registers and before any BeginPlay, for components that ask for it.
long: When an actor spawns or its level starts play, each of its components first gets OnRegister (which also runs in the editor), then every component with bWantsInitializeComponent set to true gets InitializeComponent, then the actor and its components get BeginPlay. State that other components may read in their BeginPlay, such as a stamina pool filled to full, is ready if it is set in InitializeComponent. A component registered later on an actor that is already playing gets all three steps inside its RegisterComponent call.

short: A component that draws one mesh many times, storing only a transform and a few optional floats per copy.
long: Instead of one static mesh component per rock, seat, or torch, one instanced component holds the shared mesh and material and a list of instances, each added with AddInstance as a transform. One component then stands for every copy, which saves the per-component upkeep (registration, render data, visibility checks, updates) and the memory of many separate components. Each instance can carry a few custom data floats that the material reads. The hierarchical version clusters instances so large sets cull and change detail in groups, which is what foliage uses. Instances have no tick, events, or logic of their own.

short: World space measures from the level origin; local space measures from an actor or component, along its own forward, right, and up.
long: The same numbers mean different things in the two spaces. An offset of 100 forward in world space always heads along the level's X axis; in local space it heads along wherever the actor is facing, so turning the actor turns the move. A component attached to a parent keeps a relative location and rotation, measured in its parent's space, and the engine combines the chain into the world transform. Pick the space that matches the sentence you would say aloud: "slide east" is world, "slide forward" is local.

short: Functions that move or turn an actor by a change instead of to a place, in world or local space, optionally sweeping so a blocker stops the move.
long: AddActorWorldOffset(Delta) moves the actor by Delta measured in the world; AddActorLocalOffset(Delta) measures Delta in the actor's own frame. Both take a sweep flag and an optional FHitResult: with the flag on, the move stops at the first blocking hit and the hit result says what stopped it, where, and which way the surface faces. Without it the actor is placed even inside a wall. The rotation versions turn the actor by a change the same way; they combine rotations as quaternions, so adding a small turn to an already tilted actor does what you expect. SetActorLocation and SetActorRotation instead say where the actor should end up.

short: Moving a value toward a target a little each frame, either easing out as it nears or at a constant rate.
long: The interp functions in FMath take the current value, the target, the frame's DeltaTime, and a speed, and return the value for this frame. The ease-out family (FInterpTo, VInterpTo, RInterpTo) closes a fraction of the remaining gap each frame, so it starts fast and slows as it nears, and it passes DeltaTime in so the result barely depends on the frame rate. The constant family (FInterpConstantTo, VInterpConstantTo, RInterpConstantTo) moves by a fixed amount per second and never overshoots, which makes a speed limit or a turn-rate limit. The rotator versions take the short way round. Lerp is different: it blends by an alpha you choose, with no notion of time.

short: The base class of components that move their owner, such as projectile, floating-pawn, and character movement.
long: A movement component updates one scene component, usually the owner's root, each tick, and handles the sweeping, sliding, and hit reporting that hand-written movement has to repeat. UProjectileMovementComponent flies things; UFloatingPawnMovement drifts a pawn that has no walking; UCharacterMovementComponent walks, jumps, and falls. Reach for one when the motion is a standard kind, and write your own Tick when the motion is the mechanic, such as a patrol with a rule at each end or a dart with its own turn limit.

short: A spawn parameter that starts a new actor from an existing actor's property values instead of from the class defaults.
long: FActorSpawnParameters has a Template field. Set it to an existing actor of exactly the same class and the world builds the new actor from that actor's property values, so a tuned instance becomes the starting point for any number of copies. The template is still a real actor in the world and plays like one unless you hide it and turn its collision off, and a copy takes those values too. The root component's own place is one of the values a copy takes, so a copy may not land where you asked until you set its location. A template of a different class makes the spawn fail.

short: The function that makes a separate copy of a UObject, including the objects it owns.
long: DuplicateObject takes a source object and an outer and returns a new object of the same class with the same saved property values (Transient properties are skipped). Subobjects the source owns, such as components or helper objects created inside it, are duplicated too, so the copy does not share them. Objects the source only points at stay shared between the two. It is the engine's own deep copy for objects that are not actors; actors are copied by spawning with a template. Prefer it to a hand-written Clone function that lists every field, which falls behind as soon as someone adds a field.

short: The rule that an input action which takes a key hides that key from lower priority mapping contexts.
long: Every input action has a Consume Input setting, on by default. When a higher priority mapping context maps a key to such an action, the lower priority contexts never see that key: their mappings of it are dropped when the player's mappings are rebuilt. This is how a pause or menu context stops gameplay keys without touching gameplay code, even if nothing is bound to its action. Turn the setting off on the higher action to let the key reach both layers.

short: The running state of an input action, which a handler can take to read its value and how long it has been going.
long: A handler bound with BindAction may take a const FInputActionInstance& instead of the plain value. The instance gives GetValue, GetTriggerEvent, GetElapsedTime (seconds the action has been started, ongoing, or triggered) and GetTriggeredTime (seconds spent triggered). A charge bar reads the elapsed time of a Hold action and divides it by the full charge time.

short: A small interpreter whose instructions take their inputs from the top of a stack of values and put their answer back on top.
long: Each instruction of a stack machine names what to do, not where its inputs are: an add takes the two values on top of the stack and puts their sum back. Because the order of the instructions already says what is worked out first, a formula with brackets becomes a flat list, and each instruction stays tiny. In a game the stack has a fixed size, and an instruction that needs more values than the stack holds, or would overfill it, is refused rather than trusted. Unreal's own script interpreter keeps its place in a running Blueprint function in an FFrame.

short: The part of the engine that runs compiled Blueprint graphs by reading their script bytes one token at a time.
long: When a Blueprint compiles, each graph becomes a byte array of script tokens (the EExprToken values, such as EX_Jump and EX_IntConst) stored in the Script array of its UFunction. While the game runs, the engine walks those bytes with an FFrame that remembers where it is, calling native functions and reading properties through reflection. Jumps check a runaway counter, so a loop that never ends is stopped with an error once it passes the engine's MaximumLoopIterationCount. It is why Blueprint changes need no C++ compile, and also why a tight Blueprint loop costs more than the same loop in C++.

short: A meta specifier that lets a property be edited in the Details panel only while a condition on other properties holds.
long: meta = (EditCondition = "Op == EMyOp::EMO_PushNumber") greys out the property unless the condition is true, and adding EditConditionHides hides it instead. The condition can name a bool, compare an enum property with one of its values, and combine tests with && and ||. On a struct shown as a row of an array, each row checks its own fields, so a list of steps shows a number only on the rows that push one. It changes only the editor: the property still exists and can still be set from code.

short: A parameter specifier that makes a non-const reference parameter of a Blueprint function an input that comes back changed, instead of an output only.
long: A BlueprintCallable function that takes a struct as a plain non-const reference shows it in Blueprint as an output pin only, because the engine assumes the function fills it in. Writing UPARAM(ref) before the parameter marks it as passed by reference (the CPF_ReferenceParm flag), so the node gets one pin that takes the caller's variable in, and the function's changes land in that variable. Use it when a function changes something the caller already has, such as a set of stats a potion adjusts.

short: A variable that exists once for the whole program, instead of once per object, per call, or per world.
long: A static member or a static local in C++ is made once and lives until the program closes, shared by every caller. In the Unreal editor the program is the editor itself, so a static holds its value across every Play In Editor session and is shared by every world running at the same time. A static pointer to a UObject is also invisible to the garbage collector: unless the object is rooted it can be destroyed while the pointer still holds its address, and if it is rooted it lives until the program ends. Keep statics for values that truly belong to the whole program, such as constants.

short: Puts a UObject in the root set, so the garbage collector never destroys it until RemoveFromRoot is called.
long: The garbage collector keeps every object it can reach from the root set and destroys the rest. AddToRoot adds an object to that set directly, which keeps it alive even when nothing else points at it through a UPROPERTY. It is meant for a few long-lived engine objects; in gameplay code it usually patches a static pointer, and it turns that object into one that outlives every level and play session unless something remembers to call RemoveFromRoot.

short: Handing an object the things it depends on, instead of letting it reach out and find them itself.
long: A class that is given its collaborators, through a function such as an Init or Use call, a constructor argument, or a property its owner sets, shows its dependencies in its interface and can be given a different one at any time: a practice log instead of the ranked log, or a test double in an automation test. The cost is wiring: whoever builds the object must make or find the dependency and pass it along. In Unreal, the owner that does the wiring is often a game mode, a director actor, or a subsystem that the engine creates with a known lifetime.
